abstract: The extent to which evolution proceeds predictably across environmental gradients remains a central question in modern biology. Phenotypic flexibility-the capacity for reversible responses to the environment-is one metric in which such predictability can be evaluated, as adaptation can modify the direction and degree of responses. High-elevation animals are well-suited to test how natural selection acts on flexibility, since selection pressures can be extreme and ancestral responses to such stressors are often flexible. We acclimated six taxa of Peromyscus mice spanning a gradient of native elevations (0-4,300m) to laboratory-generated hypobaria to test whether flexible responses to hypoxia have evolved predictably. We quantified responses across multiple biological levels of organization centering around oxygen transport but observed little evidence for predictable responses of aerobic performance or tissue composition. By contrast, a set of gene regulatory responses to hypoxia in skeletal muscle-the tissue responsible for shivering thermogenesis-showed predictable patterns between expression and elevation. Finally, higher elevation taxa exhibited reduced flexibility in red blood cell production and hemoglobin concentration, traits that supply oxygen to skeletal muscles. Our findings suggest that adaptation to high elevations may be frequently driven by limiting performance reductions associated with maladaptive flexibility.
